options: An element with properties between metals and nonmetals
A metal that has been melted
questions.explanation: A metalloid blends both worlds — its look, behavior, and conductivity sit between the properties of metals and nonmetals.
questions.misconception: Metalloids are real, distinct elements — not failed metals or disguised nonmetals. They have their own identity as the in-between family.

questions.prompt: Where do the metalloids sit on the periodic table?
options: Along a diagonal staircase dividing metals from nonmetals
In the center of the table only
questions.explanation: The metalloids line up along the zigzag staircase that runs diagonally down the table, separating the metal region from the nonmetal region.
questions.misconception: It's easy to imagine the families separated by a clean straight line, but the dividing line is a diagonal staircase — and the metalloids live exactly on its steps.

questions.prompt: Why is a metalloid called a semiconductor?
options: It conducts electricity only part-way and can be switched
It conducts better than any metal
It never conducts electricity at all
It conducts only heat, never electricity
questions.explanation: A semiconductor conducts part-way — between a full conductor (metal) and an insulator (nonmetal) — and can be switched on and off, which is perfect for electronics.
questions.misconception: Semiconductors aren't the best conductors (metals win that title) and they aren't insulators — their whole trick is being switchably in-between.

questions.prompt: Why is silicon, a metalloid, so important to modern technology?
options: It is a semiconductor used to build computer chips
questions.explanation: Silicon's switchable semiconduction makes it the ideal raw material for the chips in computers, phones, and nearly all electronics.
questions.misconception: Silicon isn't a metal at all and it's a solid, not a gas — its fame comes specifically from its semiconductor behavior, not from strength or appearance.
